articles.headline: WHO WILL BE THE NEXT PRESIDENT?
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: WHO WILL BE THE NEXT PRESIDENT?
articles.text:
New York—Last night, General Winfield S. Hancock became the Democratic candidate for President. He will run against Republican James A. Garfield.

Mr. Garfield promised to give government jobs to people who are good workers. Today, some people in the government give jobs to their friends.

Mr. Hancock has pledged to make the Constitution stronger.
articles.caption: James A. Garfield / Republican Candidate / President [oval engraved portrait of a bearded man]

articles.headline: MORE MILLIONAIRES
articles.text:
Topeka—There are more than 100 millionaires in America. Just 40 years ago, there were only 20 millionaires in the country.

Two of America's richest men are Andrew Carnegie, who owns many large steel companies, and John D. Rockefeller, who owns 90 percent of the nation's oil refineries.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: LET THERE BE LIGHT!
articles.text: New Jersey—Thomas Alva Edison has patented the best incandescent lamp ever. It uses a bamboo fiber sealed in a vacuum. It gives off light for 40 hours!
articles.caption: Edison's Incandescent Lamp [line drawing of an early light bulb with a threaded base]

articles.headline: ONE MILLION NEW IMMIGRANTS
articles.text:
New York — Immigrants from the British and Emerald Isles are flooding onto our shores.

Nearly 550,000 British subjects and about 440,000 Irish citizens have moved to America in the past year.

Most of the newcomers live and work in big cities on the East Coast.

Other new Americans are trying their luck out west. Some are building the railroads that spread from coast to coast. Others are plowing their homesteads in the Great Plains.

There is plenty of room for all of them here. America welcomes her cousins from across the ocean!
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: U.S. WHEAT PRODUCTION UP
articles.text:
Topeka — Mr. John W. Paton of the Kansas Farming Society reported that U.S. farmers harvested 500 million bushels of wheat this year.

Mr. Paton said that the new machine cutters have increased the harvest by 221 percent in the past 14 years.

"Farmers cut 80 percent of this year's wheat crop by machine. Only 20 percent of the crop was cut by hand."

"Unfortunately, wheat prices have dropped 27 percent since 1866."
articles.caption: [pictogram chart: three wheat sheaves of increasing size on an axis; y-axis label "500 million"; x-axis labels "1866", "1873", "1880"]

articles.headline: PRESIDENT GARFIELD IS DEAD!
articles.text:
Washington, D.C.—Two months after he was shot by Charles Jules Guiteau, President James Garfield passed away.

The president's doctors said he had fought bravely for his life, but an infection from the bullet in his back took his life.

President Garfield, a Republican, had been president for less than a year. He was forty-nine years old.

Today at noon, Vice-President Chester Arthur will be sworn in as the nation's 21st president.
articles.caption: The Late President / James A. Garfield [oval engraved portrait of a bearded man]

articles.headline: MURDERER'S STORY
articles.text:
Charles Guiteau said he shot the president to get people's attention. He believes the government usually gives jobs to people with personal connections.

Mr. Guiteau claimed that he was turned down for the job of U.S. consul in Paris "because I didn't know the right people."

If Mr. Guiteau is convicted, he will probably be executed.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: DEAF MAN "HEARS"
articles.text:
Wichita — Bob Taylor, a carpenter, was born deaf. Today, he has a new way of communicating with people.

The photophone was invented last year by Alexander Graham Bell. It turns the human voice into flashes of light that Mr. Taylor can read.

"Finally, anyone can talk to me," Mr. Taylor said, after receiving his first message.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: ALMOST ONE MILLION PEOPLE IN KANSAS
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: ALMOST ONE MILLION PEOPLE IN KANSAS
articles.text:
Kansas City—There are 632,100 more people in Kansas today than there were ten years ago.

According to the census, the state's population has climbed to 996,100.

Rain in the late 1870s was heavier than usual. The rain proved that Kansas is not a desert. This brought many farmers to our plains.

Banks helped farmers buy farms, tools, and seeds.

New barbed-wire fences kept cattle out of the fields.

Thanks to our farmers, Kansas is almost one million people strong.
articles.caption: Population in Thousands [bar chart with three gray bars: 107 (1860), 364 (1870), 996 (1880)]

articles.headline: ANGRY FARMERS DEMAND CHANGES
articles.text:
Kansas City—The Buffalo County Farmers' Alliance met here this week. Farmers from the Plains states formed the Alliance last year.

Alliance president John W. Paton said that the railroad companies charge the farmers too much to ship their grain.

"People back East are getting rich, but farmers in Kansas can't buy shoes for their children," Paton claimed.

Alliance members want the federal government to take over the railroads and the grain warehouses from the railroad companies.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: THE START OF A KANSAS DROUGHT?
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: THE START OF A KANSAS DROUGHT?
articles.text:
Salinas — Weather experts reported last week that the western Plains states may be in the first stages of a drought.

Even January's blizzard did not make up for last year's very dry summer.

This year, the spring rains were light and ended early. Two or more dry summers in a row usually means the start of a drought.

"I remember the heavy rains of 1878 and 1879," said Kansas farmer, Ben Shaker.

"Next, we had a few dry years. I would have starved if I hadn't had a windmill to water my vegetable garden."
articles.caption: Mr. Shaker's Farm [line drawing of a farm windmill beside a low farmhouse/barn]

articles.headline: ORANGE YOU GLAD
articles.text:
Last year, oranges were sent from Los Angeles, California, to the East Coast in refrigerated train cars for the first time.

The Atchison, Topeka, and the Santa Fe railway line has plans to use "cold cars" to ship Kansas crops across the country. Don't forget, you read it here first!
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: SIX HORSES IN ONE
articles.text:
Scott City — Some farmers have put a new kind of animal in front of their plows. This animal is made of steel. It is made by the Case Company.

The Case steam engine tractor has the power of six horses. The tractor easily plows even the hardest soil.

Tractors are rare today. Yet one day, they may put the plow horse out of business.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: ACT TO REGULATE COMMERCE IS LAW!
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: ACT TO REGULATE COMMERCE IS LAW!
articles.text:
Washington — Yesterday, Congress passed the Act to Regulate Commerce. This law should stop railroad companies from charging unfair prices.

The law says that prices for shipping by train must be "reasonable and just." Special rates for certain customers are not allowed.

The Act does not allow the railroads to charge more for short trips than for long ones.

"It looks like the folks in Washington are finally listening to us," said Mr. John W. Paton, president of the Buffalo County Farmers' Alliance.

Congress created a new agency, the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC).

The ICC is the first federal agency to regulate businesses. It will make sure that the railroads obey the new law.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: RANCHERS WIPED OUT BY WINTER STORMS
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: RANCHERS WIPED OUT BY WINTER STORMS
articles.text:
Scott City — Farmers and ranchers in Kansas are still estimating how much damage was caused by January's blizzards.

Thousands of cattle died, forcing many ranchers to give up their ranches. Farmers have begun to take over the old grazing grounds.

Farmers also suffered from the storms. Whole families froze or starved to death in their cabins and dugouts.
articles.caption: Heavy Snow Covers the Grasslands [silhouette drawing of two cattle standing in snow on a horizon line]

articles.headline: PRESIDENT SPEAKS AGAINST TARIFF
articles.text:
Washington, D.C.—Last week, President Cleveland told Congress why he is against the tariff.

The tariff is a tax that Americans must pay on all products made overseas.

The President explained that the tariff has made extra money for our government. The government does not spend this extra money.

"The U.S. government is not in the business of making a profit," the president said.

Benjamin Harrison, the Republican candidate for president, said that he would keep the tariff if he is elected.
articles.caption: President Grover Cleveland [oval engraved portrait of a heavy-set mustached man]

articles.headline: DRYING UP KANSAS
articles.text:
Longview — "If Kansans can drink wet, they are willing to vote dry. We've got to shut down those saloons!" declared Muriel Gale, president of the local chapter of the Women's Christian Temperence Union, last week.

An 1880 state law forbids the production and sale of alcohol in Kansas, but liquor is still easy to get here.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: DROUGHT CONTINUES
articles.text:
Salinas — Farmers, keep praying for rain! The weather forecasters say there is no sign that the drought will end soon.

Between 10 and 20 inches of rain usually fall in western Kansas each year. In the past 2 years, only 7 to 9 inches of rain have fallen each year.

Many crops have been lost. Wells cannot pump enough water to save them.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: NEW CAMERA IS "NUMBER ONE"
articles.text:
New York — Now that George Eastman has invented the "Number One" Kodak Camera, the days of the heavy camera and tripod are gone.

This camera is light enough for anyone to use, and it is well worth its $25 price tag.

When its owners finish a roll of film, they send it to the Kodak Company.

For $10, Kodak develops the pictures and sends the camera and the pictures back to their owner.

The camera is easy to use. As Mr. Eastman says, "You press the button, we do the rest."
articles.caption: The Kodak "Number One" [line drawing of a small box camera]

articles.headline: ARE CATTLE DRIVES PAST THEIR PEAK?
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: ARE CATTLE DRIVES PAST THEIR PEAK?
articles.text:
Dodge City—In the past 20 years, about 10 million head of cattle were driven north from Texas to Missouri and Kansas. Yet, ranching experts say that fewer cattle will be brought north each year.

There are 3 reasons for this: First, farmers and sheep ranchers have fenced off miles of open range. There is less room for the cattle to graze.

Secondly, refrigerated rail cars enable cows to be butchered farther away from the marketplace.

Finally, many cattle died in blizzards in the last two years.
articles.caption: Cattle Grazing [small silhouette drawing of a herd of cattle on a horizon line]

articles.headline: TWO NEW STATES JOIN THE UNION
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: TWO NEW STATES JOIN THE UNION
articles.text:
Cheyenne — On July 3, Wyoming became a state.  On July 10, Idaho became a state.

A territory must have at least 60,000 residents to apply for statehood.

Idaho has 89,000 residents.  It has an average of 1.1 people per square mile.

Only 63,000 people live in the state of Wyoming.  They are spread out at 0.6 people per square mile.

Wyoming is a state that does things its own way.  In this new state, women are allowed to vote.

The state of Kansas welcomes the 43rd and the 44th states into the United States of America.
articles.caption: (no caption) [Map of the continental United States in gray with Idaho and Wyoming filled in black; one state in the southwest shown in white]

articles.headline: NO MORE FRONTIER?
articles.text:
Washington — The U.S. Census Bureau reports that the national population has reached 63,056,000.

According to the Bureau, there is so much settlement in the West that there is no longer a "frontier line."

Those living in sparsely settled parts of Wyoming or the Oklahoma territory would surely disagree.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: TWO NEW PARKS
articles.text:
Los Angeles — Washington announced that two natural wonders in California will now be national parks.

Yosemite Park has beautiful cliffs and waterfalls carved from ancient glaciers.

In Sequoia Park, huge Redwood trees make people look as tiny as ants.

Both of these national parks are worth the trip!
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: TRUST-BUSTING IN THE UNITED STATES
articles.text:
Washington — Earlier this year, Congress passed the Sherman Anti-Trust Act.  A trust is a group of companies that work together to control a product or service, such as oil or steel.

Some farmers in the South and the Middle West think this law will not stop trusts.  They started a new political party, the People's Party.

The People's Party wants to break up trusts.

It wants the government to take over the telephone lines and railroads.

Members of the People's Party are called Populists.  They say that their party represents most Americans.

However, many Americans are afraid of the changes that the Populists want to make.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: ECONOMIC CRASH CONTINUES
articles.text:
Washington — The economic crash that started in February is getting worse.

The crash began when farmers decided to grow fewer crops because they were offered low prices.  At the same time, factories chose to make fewer products.

People became worried about the future.  They bought fewer things to save money.

Soon many companies went out of business, because not enough people wanted to buy their products.  Everyone at these companies lost their jobs.

Since February, over 15,000 companies and 500 banks have closed.  Also, 71 railroad companies have gone broke.

Experts say the economy may recover in 2 or 3 years.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: "HIGHWAY ROBBERY"
articles.text:
Topeka — Farming leader J. W. Paton spoke out against the railroad companies.

"The railroads are highway robbers," Mr. Paton said. "The farmer gets 10 cents a bushel for his crops.  Then the railroad hires dealers who resell the crops for 65 cents a bushel."

Mr. Paton, like other Populists, has called for laws against unfair prices.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: THOUSANDS GO TO CHICAGO FAIR
articles.text:
Chicago — Thousands are visiting the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

This giant fair features a Pullman train car, a phonograph, and a house where everything runs on electricity.

Adventurous visitors can ride on the big revolving wheel invented by George Ferris.

Many people are talking about the beautiful buildings at the fair, especially Daniel Burham's "White City."

Fair officials say that even though the economy is not good right now, they think that the fair will make a profit.
articles.caption: (no caption) [Black-and-white engraving of the Ferris wheel with crowds at its base]

articles.headline: A WILD OKLAHOMA LAND RUSH
articles.text:
Coffeyville — Yesterday, the gunshot rang out at high noon.

This was not a horse race.  It was the second Oklahoma land rush.  The Cherokee Outlet area was opened to settlers.  The first land rush in Oklahoma was in 1889.

The settlers rushed across the starting line on their horses and mules.  Each family staked out a good spot to start a homestead.

Shopkeepers set up tents in a central place to sell goods and tools to the new settlers. Later, they will build stores there.

In a few hours, a new town was born, and hundreds of new neighbors met for the first time.
articles.caption: The Land Rush [Black-and-white photo of a crowd of settlers in covered wagons and on horseback racing forward]

articles.headline: PULLMAN WORKERS SAY "ENOUGH!"
articles.text:
Pullman, Illinois — On May 1, workers at the Pullman Car Company went on strike.

The Pullman Company makes and services luxury passenger train cars.

The company cut its workers' wages by 28 percent because of last year's financial crash.

However, it kept charging its employees the same amount of money for rent and food.

The Pullman Company owns and runs nearly everything in this town.

At present, the strike affects only passenger trains, as Pullman employees refuse to service their company's cars.

However, a speaker for the American Railway Union (A.R.U.) said it may join the strike in June.  That would freeze railway shipping across the country.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: JOBLESS MARCH
articles.text:
Washington — Hundreds of jobless Americans marched through the city on May 1st.

A group of marchers called "Coxey's Army," led by Populist Jacob Coxey, were arrested for marching on the Capitol lawn.

Many people lost their jobs when companies closed in last year's economic crash. They marched to demand that the government find work for them.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: A NEW BALL GAME
articles.text:
Dodge City — Lately, boys in Dodge City have been throwing balls at a basket nailed to a wall.

They are playing a new game, called basketball.  It was invented three years ago by Dr. James Naismith, a teacher in Springfield, Massachusetts.

"It's lots of fun," said 10-year-old Harry Jackson. "You have to run a lot!"
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: POPULIST MEETING DRAWS A CROWD
articles.text:
Wichita — Over 200 people cheered the speech of Populist leader John W. Paton at a rally here last week.

"Four years ago, Congress passed the Sherman Anti-Trust Act," said Mr. Paton.

"This law was supposed to protect us from those big companies who get together and set high prices for things we need."

Mr. Paton claimed that the Sherman Anti-Trust Act does not work.

"Nearly every time someone sues the railroads for controlling prices, the railroads won. Now let's see what happens with this Pullman strike."

Next week, "Sockless" Jerry Simpson will speak at another Populist rally here.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: THE LAST OF THE BUFFALOES?
articles.text:
Kansas City — A recent report claims that there are fewer than 1,000 buffaloes left in the country.

Great herds of buffaloes once roamed freely across the Wild West.

Indians and white trappers killed only as many buffaloes as they could eat.

Then, railroads were built across the Great Plains.

People came west to shoot great numbers of buffaloes for sport.

Now, there are only a few of these large beasts left on the plains.  The Indians, who once relied on them for food, were forced to move to reservations.
articles.caption: A buffalo of the Great Plains [Black-and-white engraving of a shaggy buffalo standing, side view]

- **Bottom headline (two columns):** WILLIAM TAFT - A "SURE THING" FOR PRESIDENT
- **Bottom-right box (ads):** identical to 1894 front page ("The [illegible]" / "First Class [illegible] Food and Drink / Right in the Center of Topeka" with small standing-man figure / "[illegible name]" / "ATTORNEY AT LAW").

articles.headline: THE ENLARGED HOMESTEAD ACT IS PASSED
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: THE ENLARGED HOMESTEAD ACT IS PASSED
articles.text:
Washington — The U.S. government has doubled the amount of land that it gives to homesteaders.

Congress passed the Enlarged Homestead Act, which allows farmers to claim 320 acres of land.

The Homestead Act of 1862 gave farmers 160 acres.

Plains farmers have wanted this change for many years.

"It's just impossible for a farmer to squeeze a living out of only 160 dry, hard acres," said Kansas farmer Larry Finster.  "There's not enough water here!"

Many homesteaders have already found ways to enlarge their farms, sometimes not exactly according to the law.

Now, they can add to their farms legally.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: ONLY THE MODEL T
articles.text:
Detroit — The Ford Motor Company has announced that its factory will produce only the Model T car.

The Model T is a sturdy car that is popular with the average American.  Some farmers even use Model T's to pull their tractors.

The Ford company said that as production costs drop, it will reduce the $850 price tag on the Model T.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: WILL THE ARMY FLY?
articles.text:
Wichita — The U.S. Army has bought a flying machine from Orville and Wilbur Wright.

On December 17, 1903, the brothers made their first successful flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

Since then, they have been working hard to improve their flying machine, which runs on gas.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: PEARY AND HIS TEAM REACH THE NORTH POLE
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: PEARY AND HIS TEAM REACH THE NORTH POLE
articles.text:
Kansas City — On April 6, the dream of a lifetime came true for explorer Robert E. Peary.  He reached the North Pole.

Peary traveled with his Negro assistant, Matthew Henson, and four Eskimos. The team made their journey in a sled that was pulled by dogs.

Mr. Peary has been on many trips to the Arctic in the past 20 years.  When he finally reached the North Pole he wrote, "I cannot bring myself to realize it."
articles.caption: Ice caves near the North Pole [Grayscale photo of large ice formations with cave-like arches]

articles.headline: WILLIAM TAFT — A "SURE THING" FOR PRESIDENT
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: WILLIAM TAFT — A "SURE THING" FOR PRESIDENT
articles.text:
Washington — Last year, President Roosevelt let everyone know that he wanted William Howard Taft to be the next president. Since then, people have been saying that Taft's election is a "sure thing."

Mr. Taft started out as a very respected federal judge. Next, he was the governor of the Philippines.  Then he became Secretary of War.

Many people say that Mr. Taft won the Republican nomination because of President Roosevelt.

Kansans tend to vote mostly Republican. However, many Populists in Kansas may vote for William Jennings Bryan, the "free silver" Democratic candidate.


# Newspaper transcriptions — 1914, 1915, 1917, 1919
articles.caption: William H. Taft [Oval engraved portrait of Taft]

articles.headline: BRITAIN DECLARES WAR ON GERMANY
articles.text:
London, ENGLAND — Last night, Great Britain declared war on Germany.
This followed Germany's threat to send its troops through Belgium on their way to attack France.
Belgium wanted to stay neutral in the war in Europe. However, Belgium refused to let German troops cross its border.
Yesterday, Germany began bombing the Belgian countryside as part of its invasion of that small country.
Experts predict that the war will harm European livestock and crops.
articles.caption: (no caption) [A map with these labels: North Sea, Holland, England, Belgium, Germany (written vertically), France. England and the sea are shaded grey.]

articles.headline: COUNTRIES AT WAR
articles.text:
Paris, FRANCE — Eight nations are now fighting in Europe.
Germany and Austria-Hungary are at war against England, Belgium, France, Russia, Serbia, and Montenegro.
Italy, Switzerland, and Holland are preparing their troops for war, although they say they will remain neutral.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: FIRST YEAR OF NEW TAX
articles.text:
Kansas City — Kansas citizens have sent in their forms to pay taxes on the money they earned in 1913.
Last year, the 16th Amendment was ratified. That gave the government the right to tax our income.
Most people will pay tax on one percent of their income. People who make more than $20,000 a year will pay up to six percent income tax.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: HOW THE WAR IN EUROPE STARTED
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: HOW THE WAR IN EUROPE STARTED
articles.text:
London, ENGLAND — For the past 25 years, many European nations have been in conflict without actually being at war.
These nations compete against each other to set up new colonies in Africa and the Middle East.
Some nations have signed treaties. If one nation in a treaty is attacked, the other nations must defend it.
In the southern part of Austria-Hungary, there are many Serbs who want their land to be part of Serbia.
On June 28, one of these Serbs killed the Archduke of Austria-Hungary and his wife. Later, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.
Because of the treaties between European countries, many nations have become involved in the war.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: THE PANAMA CANAL IS OPEN FOR BUSINESS
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: THE PANAMA CANAL IS OPEN FOR BUSINESS
articles.text:
Panama City, PANAMA — After ten years of hard work, the Panama Canal is ready for its first customer.
Next week the S.S. Ancon will sail from the Atlantic to the Pacific through the new canal.
The canal cuts through the narrowest part of Panama, and connects the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
The country of Panama is a narrow strip of land that connects North America and South America.
Soon cargo and passenger ships will travel between the oceans without going around the tip of South America. This was a 13,000-mile trip.
Soon it will be easier for the U.S. Navy to protect our islands in the Pacific Ocean.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: THE PRESIDENT: "TOO PROUD TO FIGHT"
articles.text:
Washington — In response to calls to declare war, President Wilson said, "We are too proud to fight."
Emotions are running high as details of the attack on the Lusitania become known.
The Lusitania was on its way from the United States to England when the Germans sank it in May. More than 100 Americans died.
Many people want the president to declare war on Germany.
The president continues to protest to the German government. Former president Theodore Roosevelt and Secretary of State Bryan say that protests will not stop the Germans from sinking more ships. They say protests will not keep us out of the war.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: INNOCENT VICTIMS
articles.text:
London, ENGLAND—There were 1,919 people on board the Lusitania when a German U-boat torpedoed the ship.
Most passengers on this unarmed British ship were American or British. On May 17, the cold Atlantic claimed 1,198 innocent lives.
articles.caption: Where the ship went down [A dithered grey map with the labels IRELAND and ENGLAND. An arrow points to an X off the southern coast of Ireland.]

articles.headline: ITALY JOINS THE FIGHT!
articles.text:
Rome — On May 23, Italy declared war on Austria-Hungary. It has broken its partnership with that nation and with Germany.
Italy joined France, England, and other nations in the fight against Germany and Austria-Hungary.
Many farmers in Europe cannot work their fields. If the war continues, many Europeans may go hungry.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: RUSH TO PUMP BLACK GOLD IN WICHITA
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: RUSH TO PUMP BLACK GOLD IN WICHITA
articles.text:
Wichita — Prospectors have struck oil in nearby fields.
Now, more prospectors are making their way to Wichita. They are buying drilling equipment and starting to drill for oil.
Wichita has been a lively town for some time. The Chisholm Trail and the railroad have increased the population.
"I don't care if these prospectors find oil," said Robert "Rail" Stone, owner of the Wichita General Store. "I'm just glad they buy their gear in my store."
Mr. Stone first came to Wichita many years ago when he worked on the railroad.
Now he is thought of as an "old-timer" by the new oil seekers in Wichita.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: NATIONAL TREASURES OF THE WILD WEST
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: NATIONAL TREASURES OF THE WILD WEST
articles.text:
Denver — The federal government has set aside the most scenic part of the Rocky Mountains as the Rocky Mountain National Park.
Many years ago, glaciers carved beautiful mountains out of the rocks. The highest mountain is Longs Peak, which is 14,256 feet tall.
Now that this area is a national park, it will be preserved.
In central Arizona, ancient Pueblo Indian cliff houses will be preserved in the new Walnut Canyon National Monument. The Pueblo Indians lived there about 1,000 years ago.
articles.caption: A Colorado mountain range [A dithered black-and-white photo of a rocky mountain peak.]

articles.headline: AMERICA DECLARES WAR ON GERMANY!
articles.text:
Washington — Congress voted today to declare war on Germany. Apparently, our senators and representatives agree with President Wilson. He said, "The world must be made safe for democracy."
On April 2, the president asked Congress to declare war on Germany.
The president said that Germany is already at war with the United States.
German U-boats have been sinking unarmed Allied ships for the past three years. Over 200 Americans have died in these attacks.
Now America will start fighting back!
articles.caption: President Wilson [An oval engraved portrait of Woodrow Wilson in a suit, head and shoulders.]

articles.headline: ARMY CALL-UP SOON
articles.text:
Washington — War has just been declared, and Americans are already talking about who will fight.
The government is expected to begin a call-up of men between the ages of 21 and 30 shortly. The enlisted men will receive a short but practical training course.
Then, our soldiers will be on their way to Europe to win the war.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: ESCAPE FROM RUSSIA
articles.text:
Topeka — Kansan Tom Graham has finally come home from Moscow. Mr. Graham is an agent for the U.S. government, which is selling grain to the Russians.
In March, there was an uprising against the Russian czar. As a result, it took one month for Mr. Graham to get out of the country.
"I hope I can go back when it's safer," he said. "The Russians still need our grain."
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: KANSAS FARMERS TO HELP WAR EFFORT
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: KANSAS FARMERS TO HELP WAR EFFORT
articles.text:
Kansas City — "Kansas will be an important source of wheat for our hungry allies in war-torn Europe," said Mr. Paul Paton, a representative of the Buffalo County Farmers' Alliance.
Mr. Paton's father, John, was Alliance president and a People's Party member until the party collapsed in 1908.
"If we don't send our grain to France and Belgium soon, people there will starve," Paul Paton said. "Americans need to buckle down, work hard, and make sacrifices."
Today's declaration of war by Congress makes it more important than ever to help the war effort. Folks in Kansas will do their best!
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: A VERY SPECIAL TOWN IN NEBRASKA
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: A VERY SPECIAL TOWN IN NEBRASKA
articles.text:
Omaha — A new village has been founded on about 1700 acres of farmland in eastern Nebraska.
The village is Boys Town, where homeless boys between the ages of 10 and 18 are given a new start in life.
Father Edward Joseph Flanagan, a Catholic priest, founded Boys Town.
He wanted to change the lives of boys who had lost hope in their future.
At Boys Town, former gang members learn to be responsible leaders. Boys who have dropped out of school receive an education.
The boys run the town themselves, under the watchful eye of Father Flanagan.
articles.caption: none. The image has stray dot artifacts near "themselves," and "the".

articles.headline: WILSON AT PEACE CONFERENCE
articles.text:
Paris, FRANCE — On January 18, President Wilson will attend the Paris Peace Conference.
At the conference, the 32 Allied nations will prepare a peace treaty for Germany to sign.
The Germans want the Allies to base the treaty on a 14-point peace plan that President Wilson published on January 8.
The plan includes creating a League of Nations to keep world peace.
However, the other Allied leaders do not support the plan. They want a treaty that will punish Germany for having started the war. They think this will stop Germany from starting another war.
The president hopes to persuade the Allied leaders to accept at least part of his plan.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: POSTWAR RELIEF BILL
articles.text:
Washington — Congress has approved the spending of $100,000,000 for relief work in Europe.
The money will help rebuild destroyed cities and supply basic goods and medicines.
The United States will give free food to whoever cannot pay because of the war.
America will continue to rescue her European allies!
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: WILL THE U.S. GO DRY?
articles.text:
Topeka — Prohibitionists are hoping to celebrate with a sip of soda water, not champagne.
In a few days, the states will finish voting on the Eighteenth Amendment. If the amendment is passed, it will be illegal to sell alcohol everywhere in America.
In some states, it is already against the law to sell alcohol. Kansas was one of the first states to pass prohibition laws, back in 1880.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: TEDDY ROOSEVELT -- THE LIGHT IS OUT
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: TEDDY ROOSEVELT -- THE LIGHT IS OUT
articles.text:
Oyster Bay, N.Y. — "Put out the light, please," were Theodore Roosevelt's last words before he passed away early yesterday.
The popular former president had been ill for some time. He never fully recovered from the tropical fevers he caught during a 1914 trip to the jungles of Brazil.
The war death of his son, Quentin, in 1918, was also very difficult for him.
Louis J. Wilde, the mayor of San Diego, said, "All the world loved 'Teddy.'"
Our beloved President Roosevelt improved our country and got things done.
He will be buried in a nearby cemetery, without a large ceremony.
articles.caption: none

articles.headline: WHEN WILL JOHN MARCH HOME AGAIN?
articles.headlineOnFrontPage: WHEN WILL JOHN MARCH HOME AGAIN?
articles.text:
Abilene — "When will my boy come home?" Abilene native Harriet Driver asked.
Mrs. Driver is still waiting for her only son, John, to return home from the war.
Mrs. Driver runs her 320-acre farm with only hired help. Her husband died in last year's Spanish Influenza epidemic that took nearly half a million American lives.
Mrs. Driver's brother, Frank, died in 1912. He was a passenger aboard the ship, the Titanic, which struck an iceberg and sank.
Officials in Washington say it will be months before all the soldiers return home.

---
articles.caption: John Driver and his late father, in 1912 [A small dithered photo of two men, head and shoulders. One wears a cap.]
